Substitutionary
sub-sti-too´shun-er-ee
adj. (of the atonement: Christ suffered in the room and stead of His people, the just for the unjust)
Latin substituere, to put one in the place of another, from sub- under + statuere to set. The Bible's preposition is for — anti, hyper — a life given in the place of many.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Substitutionary names the heart of the atonement: Christ suffered in the place of sinners, bearing what was due to them, that they might receive what is due to Him. Isaiah said it before the word existed: “he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed” (Isa 53:5). Paul gives the exchange in one sentence: “For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him” (2Co 5:21). Peter makes the parties explicit: “Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God” (1Pe 3:18). The curse is not waived. It is borne: “Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us” (Gal 3:13). And the Son of man states His own errand: “to give his life a ransom for many” (Mar 10:45). This is not one theory on a shelf with moral influence and governmental display. Those may describe fruits. They do not explain the wounds.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines substitution as the act of putting one person or thing in the place of another to supply its place; as the substitution of an agent, attorney or representative to act for one in his absence.

expand to see more

SUBSTITU'TION, n. The act of putting one person or thing in the place of another to supply its place;

as the substitution of an agent, attorney or representative to act for one in his absence;

the substitution of bank notes for gold and silver, as a circulating medium.

1. In grammar, syllepsis, or the use of one word for another.

Key Scripture

Isa 53:5 — "But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed."

2Co 5:21 — "For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him."

1Pe 3:18 — "For Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God, being put to death in the flesh, but quickened by the Spirit:"

Gal 3:13 — "Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us: for it is written, Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree:"

Mar 10:45 — "For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many."

Modern Corruption

The wounds are turned into an example of love, or a display to the universe, anything except a penalty borne in another man's room.

expand to see more

Moral-influence readings keep the love and empty the justice. Christ dies to show how much God cares, and the sinner is moved to repent. Isaiah 53 will not go into that mold. The chastisement of our peace was upon him. Wounded for our transgressions is not wounded to inspire us. A display that does not bear anything leaves the guilt where it was.

Governmental and exemplary theories do the same work with more dignity. God must show that He hates sin, so He makes a public example of His Son. Peter says the just suffered for the unjust, that He might bring us to God. The preposition is substitution, not theatre. And Galatians 3:13 is still more stubborn: He was made a curse for us. An example is not made a curse. A substitute is.

The ransom word is particular. A ransom for many, not a potential payment left on the table for whoever will pick it up. The dictionary's standard is definite atonement: the work effectually for the elect. Universalizing the substitution until it substitutes for no one in particular is how the doctrine is kept as a slogan and lost as a gospel.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek anti (G473), in place of; hyper (G5228), on behalf of; lytron (G3083), ransom; Hebrew chalal (H2490), to wound; the Servant songs' for.

expand to see more

Greek lytron anti pollōn (G3083, G473) — a ransom for many; Mark 10:45, Matthew 20:28.

Greek hyper hēmōn hamartia (G5228) — sin for us; 2 Corinthians 5:21.

Hebrew mecholal mipeshaenu — wounded for our transgressions; Isaiah 53:5, the for that carries the gospel.

Usage

"“The just for the unjust” — the parties are named, and the direction is one way."

"“Made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin” — the exchange, not a demonstration."

"“A ransom for many” — paid, not merely priced."
